title: Everyday Hebrew
hookLine: todah, b'ezrat Hashem, mazal tov, l'chaim

lines: A PHONE CALL: A BABY GIRL.
cards: A grandmother hangs up the phone in her kitchen. Good news: the baby has arrived, a girl, and everyone is well. Within a minute the room has said four things.
Mazal tov, from everyone at once. B'ezrat Hashem, from the grandmother, when someone asks when they'll get to visit. Someone finds a bottle, pours, and lifts a glass: l'chaim.

And when the glass is handed across the table, a quiet todah. None of it is a prayer service. It's just a kitchen, with Hebrew doing a lot of work in it, and the smallest of the four carries a whole root inside.

teach.b: Everyday Hebrew, one phrase at a time. First, mazal tov. People say it at a birth, a wedding, a new job, a finished exam.
It works like congratulations; mazal is usually translated luck or fortune, and tov is good.
Second, b'ezrat Hashem: with the help of the Name, the Hashem you met two days ago.
Some Jews tuck it into talk about the future, when they'll visit, when the house will be finished, a small way of saying the plans aren't only theirs.
Third, l'chaim, to life: the same chai you added up yesterday, eighteen. Fourth, todah, thank you.
It's the plainest of the four, and its root runs back into Genesis: yod, dalet, heh, carrying thanks and acknowledgment. You met Leah's sons in year one.
When she gives birth to yet another, she says, "Now will I praise the LORD: therefore she called his name Judah."
In Hebrew, Yehudah, from the same root as todah. The psalm that repeats its refrain verse after verse opens with it too: "O give thanks unto the LORD; for he is good." In Hebrew, hodu.
And the short prayer some Jews say on waking, before anything else, begins modeh ani: I give thanks. Same root again.
So the word for passing the salt shares its root with the name Leah gave a son, and with the first word of a morning prayer. Todah.

how: Jews say mazal tov at good news, l'chaim over a raised glass, b'ezrat Hashem about plans for the future, and todah for thank you; some begin each morning with modeh ani, I give thanks, before anything else.

o: the modern Hebrew spoken only on Israeli streets

p: with the help of the Name
to life, over a raised glass

games.q: you're Leah, and you have just given birth to another son. what do you name him?
o: a name that means a son at last.
Yehudah, Judah, because now I will praise the LORD.
a name that means my husband will love me now.
games.why: "Now will I praise the LORD: therefore she called his name Judah." the same root gives Hebrew its everyday word for thank you, todah.

practice: Bring to mind one person who did something for you this week that you never properly thanked, a ride, a text, a door held, and say the word silently toward them: todah.

Then a second person, then something that isn't a person at all: the bed you slept in, the water in the tap, the breath you're taking now. If you pray, you can say modeh ani, I give thanks, the way some Jews begin each morning.

wordCard.voice: Everyday Hebrew. Mazal tov, b'ezrat Hashem, l'chaim, and todah, thank you, from the root of Judah's name. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: thank you, from yod, dalet, heh, the root of hodu, give thanks, and of the name Yehudah.

carryVoice: Your line: todah. Passing the salt and Leah's praise, all in one small root. Until tomorrow.
